links.outcome: Performance with adult vendor threshold versus locally optimized pediatric threshold
links.effect: Optimized pediatric cut-off 44.5 vs adult 15: accuracy 89.8% (vs 83.4%), specificity 92.4% (vs 82.3%), sensitivity 80.0% (vs 87.5%), similar AUC 0.93; PPV improved.
links.quote: Compared to the adult threshold, the pediatric-specific cut-off led to improvement in the specificity and the PPV, supporting a safer AI interpretation in children with a slight trade-off in the sensitivity at 80%.

links.outcome: Performance of adult-trained tool applied to pediatric population outside intended use
links.effect: Overall AUC 0.94 (sens 87.5%, spec 82.3%, PPV 56.6%) in children 2-14, but significantly lower in ages 2-6 (AUC 0.91) than 7-14 (AUC 0.96), p<0.001.
links.quote: In the older age group (n = 449 [46.9%]; mean age 10.2 ± 2 years), the performance metrics were as follows: AUC 0.96 (95% CI: 0.94–0.98), accuracy 89.7% (95% CI: 86.5–92.4%), sensitivity 86.2%, specificity 90.3%, PPV 56.8% and NPV 97.8%, respectively, which were significantly higher compared to the younger age groups (p < 0.001).

links.outcome: Performance difference between adult development population and pediatric deployment population
links.effect: Tool trained on adult radiographs; performance lower in younger children (AUC 0.91 in 2-6 vs 0.96 in 7-14, p<0.001), attributed to different anatomy.
links.quote: Notably, subanalyses by age revealed a significantly higher performance for older children aged 7–14 years, compared to younger patients (2–6 years), presumably due to a substantially different anatomy in younger individuals.

links.outcome: Subgroup performance by age group, masked by aggregate metrics
links.effect: AUC 0.91 (accuracy 78%) in ages 2-6 vs AUC 0.96 (accuracy 89.7%) in ages 7-14, p<0.001.
links.quote: In the younger age group (n = 509 [53.1%]; mean age 3.7 ± 1.4 years), the AUC for the presence of any relevant finding was 0.91 (95% CI: 0.88–0.94), with an accuracy of 78% (95% CI: 74.1–81.5%) and a sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of 88.1%, 74%, 57% and 94.1%, respectively.

links.outcome: Reference standard construction with blinded reads and consensus adjudication
links.effect: Dedicated reading separate from AI output avoided bias versus prior study; single-reader reference with consensus for discordance; authors note lack of multi-reader panel as limitation.
links.quote: We conducted a dedicated reading session informed by clinical information and radiological expertise, followed by a separate assessment of the AI-tools performance to avoid any potential bias.
